title: Subqueries and CTEs

spans.text: “Subqueries and CTEs” is a tool for solving a concrete programming problem. Identify the input and desired result, then trace what role the construct plays in the example. Study it not only as syntax, but also for its effects on readability, correctness, resource use, and future changes.
QUESTION: What will this example do? Predict the result first.

spans.code:
WITH course_counts AS (
  SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS learners
  FROM enrollments
  GROUP BY course_id
)
SELECT course_id, learners
FROM course_counts
WHERE learners >= 2;

spans.text: First counts enrollments by course, then returns courses with at least two learners.

A subquery runs inside another query. A WITH clause names an intermediate result as a common table expression (CTE), making a complex query easier to read in stages. A CTE is usually scoped to one statement; it is not automatically a persistent or materialized table.

Key line: `WITH course_counts AS (`
What it does: First counts enrollments by course, then returns courses with at least two learners.
Why it is used: Give each CTE a meaningful name and inspect intermediate results one step at a time.
If omitted or changed: A CTE can improve readability, but it is not guaranteed to be faster on every database.
